Class enumeration

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/enumeration.Rmd
enumeration.Rmd

Finite mixture models represent heterogeneity through a specified number of latent components. In latent profile analysis, components describe patterns in continuous indicators; in latent class analysis, they describe categorical response probabilities. Two-level models additionally represent differences between groups through latent group classes. For course enrolments nested within students, observation-level profiles describe engagement patterns, while group classes describe differences in the probabilities of those patterns across students. The analyst specifies the number of components at each level before estimation.

Class enumeration compares alternative numbers of components. Ordinary chi-squared likelihood ratio approximations generally do not apply when comparing different numbers of mixture components because the usual regularity conditions fail. A parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test provides a simulation-based alternative for supported models, but requires repeated fitting and careful assessment of convergence. Information criteria provide complementary comparisons by balancing log likelihood against a penalty for model complexity. These procedures can favour different numbers of classes; their performance depends on the model and data. See Nylund, Asparouhov, and Muthén (2007) for a simulation study of class-enumeration methods.

An information criterion may continue to decrease throughout the candidate range. This can reflect unresolved heterogeneity or departures from the measurement model rather than a clearly defined set of substantive classes. In two-level models, the numbers of profiles and group classes must be considered jointly. The sample-size convention used in BIC also matters: the package reports variants based on groups and observations. Classification separation, convergence, sensitivity to starting values, and the substantive interpretation of the classes provide additional evidence.

This vignette uses enumerate_classes() to fit a grid of two-level latent profile models. It examines information criteria, changes between adjacent candidates, descriptive curve summaries, classification diagnostics, and estimation diagnostics. Selected models are compared and a fitted candidate is extracted for further analysis. No single statistic is treated as a conclusive estimate of the number of classes.

library(latents)

Data

The examples use course_engagement, a simulated data frame in long format with one row per course enrolment. It contains 1,422 enrolments of 106 students. Five measures of activity in each course serve as indicators: browsing of the course site, lecture viewing, reading of the forum, posting to the forum and attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course, so a value of zero is the course average. The column student identifies the student to whom each enrolment belongs.

head(course_engagement)

Enrolments are nested in students. The profiles therefore describe patterns of activity in a single course, and the group classes describe students by how their enrolments are distributed across those patterns.

Fitting the candidate models

The candidates are fitted with enumerate_classes() from the data, the indicators in vars and the group identifier in id. The arguments n_profiles and n_group_classes give the numbers of classes to try, and one model is fitted for every combination of them. Here the numbers of profiles run from one to six and the numbers of group classes from one to four. The argument model sets the covariance structure of the profiles. The value "VVI" gives every profile its own variances and fixes the covariances at zero. Without model, the four basic structures are fitted for every combination.

Mixture likelihoods can have multiple local maxima, so each candidate is estimated from several starting values. The n_starts argument controls the number of fully fitted starts and seed controls reproducibility. This example uses three starts per candidate to limit computation. An applied analysis should assess whether increasing the number of starts changes the selected likelihood or substantive conclusions.

A Gaussian component can concentrate around very few observations and approach a variance bound. The boundary = "exclude" option excludes starts with variances at the configured bound; it does not detect every narrowly concentrated component. The latents_thin_profiles warning flags limited posterior support relative to the number of profile-specific Gaussian parameters. This is a diagnostic heuristic rather than an identification test. Inspect component sizes and covariance diagnostics before interpreting such a profile.

The default search depends on the covariance specification. EII, EEI and EEE models use emEM screening, which performs short EM runs for a larger pool of starts before completing selected candidates. Other covariance structures use k-means initialization by default. The search argument can override these defaults. The cores argument permits parallel candidate fitting.

activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
#> Warning: Profile 4: 4.9 Gaussian membership mass for 10 free means and variances. This is a

The result holds 24 fitted candidates. Each candidate is named by its numbers of profiles and group classes, so that profiles4_groups3 has four profiles and three group classes, and the name identifies the candidate in every function that follows. The 3 candidates with one profile and several group classes could not be estimated. Group classes are defined by differences in the distribution of profiles, and a model with a single profile has no such differences. These candidates remain in the table with the error that stopped them.

The table of candidates

The table of candidates has one row per candidate and is returned by as.data.frame().

The columns fall into groups.

Columns Content
candidate, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model Identity of the candidate
log_likelihood, n_parameters Fit and size
aic, kic, bic_*, sabic_*, caic_*, awe_*, icl_*, clc_* Information criteria
profile_entropy, group_entropy Relative entropy at each level
avepp_min, avepp_max, avepp_mean, avepp_below Average posterior probability of the profiles
group_avepp_min, group_avepp_max, group_avepp_mean, group_avepp_below Average posterior probability of the group classes
converged, boundary, n_best_replicated, warnings, error Checks of the estimation

Information criteria

Many information criteria combine deviance (minus twice the maximized log likelihood) with a penalty for the number of estimated parameters. Some criteria also penalize classification uncertainty. Lower values are preferred under the chosen criterion. In a two-level model, several parameter penalties depend on the sample-size convention. Criteria ending in _groups count the 106 students as the independent units, and criteria ending in _individual count the 1,422 enrolments. An analysis uses one of the two conventions throughout.

ICL and AWE include uncertainty about both the students’ group classes and their enrolments’ profiles under either convention. Changing the sample-size convention changes the parameter penalty, not which classification uncertainty is included.

The candidate at the minimum of each criterion:

get_results(models, "best")
#>    criterion  convention         candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16703
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles4_groups4          4               4   VVI 16769
#> 3        bic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16852
#> 4        bic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 16973
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16661
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16823
#> 7       caic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16903
#> 8       caic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 17011
#> 9        awe      groups profiles2_groups2          2               2   VVI 17292
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups2          2               2   VVI 17412
#> 11       icl      groups profiles2_groups3          2               3   VVI 17115
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups2          2               2   VVI 17176
#> 13       clc      groups profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 16997
#> 14       clc individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 16997

The criteria disagree. With students as the units, the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) is lowest for profiles4_groups3, the integrated completed likelihood (ICL) for profiles2_groups3 and the approximate weight of evidence (AWE) for profiles2_groups2. With enrolments as the units, BIC is lowest for profiles3_groups3. The Akaike information criterion (AIC) is lowest for profiles6_groups4, the largest candidate fitted in this example.

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, one line per number of group classes, with the lowest value of each criterion ringed.

plot_enumeration(models)

A minimum at the largest candidate leaves uncertainty about models beyond the fitted range. Consider a wider, scientifically plausible range alongside alternative measurement and covariance specifications. An interior minimum is not guaranteed. Any criterion can be plotted by name; what = "all" displays every criterion.

plot_enumeration(models, what = "bic_groups")

The tree summarizes correspondence between profiles across independently fitted models. Links are weighted by shared posterior membership mass, computed from products of the models’ membership probabilities, rather than by assuming that profiles form nested partitions. Each number of group classes has its own tree, and n_group_classes selects one; plot_tree(models) returns them all, one plot each. The guide Tree plot compares solutions at one number of profiles and plots the tree of group classes.

plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)

Change with each added class

When a criterion decreases across the whole candidate range, successive changes help describe how much each additional class improves that criterion. For every candidate, the table reports the decrease in BIC from the candidate with one profile fewer and the same number of group classes, and the decrease from the candidate with one group class fewer and the same number of profiles. A positive value means that the added class lowered the criterion. The argument using selects another criterion.

With three group classes, adding a third profile lowers BIC by 85 and adding a fourth lowers it by 22. Adding a fifth profile raises BIC by 27, which appears in the table as a negative decrease. The decreases are plotted for both directions, along the number of profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the right.

plot_selection(models, what = "deltas")

The knee summary scales both axes of a curve to the unit interval and finds the candidate with the largest perpendicular distance below the straight line from the first point to the last. This chord-distance rule is inspired by Kneedle, without its smoothing or sensitivity thresholds. A nearly linear curve can have a very small maximum distance, so the reported distance describes the strength of the bend as well as its location. The knee is computed along the number of profiles for each number of group classes, along the number of group classes for each number of profiles, and across all candidates ordered by their number of parameters.

get_results(models, "knees")

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is profiles4_groups3. The straight line ends at the largest candidate, so the knee depends on the range fitted. Without the largest candidate the knee is profiles3_groups3, which the table records in stable and note. Along the number of group classes with four profiles, the knee is profiles4_groups2.

The heatmap displays each candidate’s criterion value relative to the minimum across the fitted grid:

plot_selection(models, what = "heatmap")

Classification quality

Every observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class. Relative entropy summarizes these probabilities over all observations, from 0 when every observation is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1 when every observation belongs to one class with certainty. The average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that class among the observations assigned to it. Higher AvePP values indicate greater posterior certainty within the assigned class. The candidate table reports the lowest, highest and mean AvePP at each level and the number of classes below a user-selected cutoff (cutoff, default 0.8). This threshold is a descriptive screening choice, not a validated criterion for selecting the number of classes.

plot_selection(models, what = "diagnostics")

For profiles4_groups3, the relative entropy is 0.74 for the profiles and 0.82 for the group classes. The lowest AvePP is 0.8 among the profiles and 0.86 among the group classes.

Checks of the estimation

Replication of the selected likelihood across starts provides evidence of numerical stability, but cannot establish that the global maximum has been found. Boundary estimates and small components warrant investigation because they can indicate a solution driven by limited support or a restrictive parameter bound. Their interpretation depends on the fitted model and data. Refitting with boundary = "exclude" selects among starts whose continuous variance parameters are above their lower bounds. This option changes start selection and does not by itself establish that the retained components are substantively meaningful. The following plots summarize these diagnostics.

plot_selection(models, what = "trust")

plot_selection(models, what = "smallest")

All of the plots for choosing the number of classes are produced together with plot_selection(models).

Comparing candidates

Selected candidates are placed side by side with compare_models(). Candidates are named as in the table, given by their numbers of classes, or selected by a number of profiles or group classes. The comparison adds the difference in BIC from the lowest of the candidates compared and the BIC weight. The weight is exp(-delta_bic / 2) normalized over the compared candidates. It summarizes relative support under this BIC approximation and depends on the candidate set; it should not be interpreted as a calibrated probability that a model is correct.

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

compare_models(models, bic_groups_pick, icl_groups_pick, awe_groups_pick)
#> Model comparison

Analysis of the chosen candidate

The example continues with profiles4_groups3, the candidate with the lowest BIC with students as the units. It is taken from the fitted candidates by name with get_candidate(). The numbers of classes give the same model, as in get_candidate(models, 4, 3).

chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen

The profiles are plotted as their means on the five indicators.

plot_profiles(chosen)

Each group class of students has its own distribution of the four profiles.

plot_prevalence(chosen)

The classification diagnostics of the chosen model:

diagnostics(chosen)

plot_diagnostics(chosen)

Each enrolment with its profile, its student’s group class and its posterior probabilities:

head(get_results(chosen, "assignments", data = course_engagement))

The profiles can also be related to an external variable. The following analysis uses three_step() to estimate profile-specific means of previous_grade, with BCH correction for classification error. The variable precedes the course enrolment, so these comparisons describe associations rather than effects of profile membership on grades.

three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
#> Distal outcome by class (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class   Mean          95% CI     SE  Effective n
#> -----  -----  --------------  -----  -----------
#>     1   0.17  [ 0.07,  0.27]  0.050       338.48
#>     2  -0.37  [-0.53, -0.20]  0.084       111.09
#>     3  -0.30  [-0.41, -0.18]  0.058       256.17
#>     4   0.31  [ 0.18,  0.45]  0.069       210.62

Functions

Call Result
enumerate_classes(data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model) The fitted candidate models
as.data.frame(models) One row per candidate with every column
get_results(models, “best”) The candidate at the minimum of each criterion
get_results(models, “classification”) Size, AvePP and entropy of every class of every candidate
get_results(models, “candidates”, cutoff = 0.9) The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff
get_results(models, “deltas”, using = ) Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer
get_results(models, “knees”, using = ) Maximum chord-distance knee of each line, its range and its stability
plot_enumeration(models), plot_enumeration(models, what = “bic_groups”), what = “all” Information criteria across the candidates
plot_tree(models) Division of profiles as more are added
plot_enumeration(models, what = “entropy”, “avepp” or “diagnostics”, cutoff = ) Entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates
plot_selection(models, what = “deltas”, “heatmap”, “smallest” or “trust”, using = ) Decreases, distance from the lowest criterion, smallest class, estimation checks
plot_selection(models) All of the plots for choosing the number of classes
get_candidate(models, “profiles4_groups3”), get_candidate(models, 4, 3) One fitted candidate
compare_models(models, “name”, c(4, 2), …) Named candidates side by side
compare_models(models, n_profiles = , n_group_classes = ) All candidates with the given numbers of classes
compare_models(name = fit, name = fit) Fitted models side by side, on the same data
get_candidate(comparison, “name”) The model behind a row of a comparison
get_results(comparison, “classification”) Every class of every compared model
